title: Butter in My Coffee: How a Dinner with an Old Friend Changed Everything This Chemist Knew
description: Back pain since high school. Weight, fatigue, fog on top of it. All of it blamed on aging. At 66 I changed what I ate. Within a year it was gone. At 71 it has not come back. You were probably told it was your fault. The weight that won’t come off. The fatigue. The aches, the fog, the slow decline you were told to accept as the price of aging. Eat less, try harder. If you’ve done everything right and gotten sicker anyway, some part of you already knows that story doesn’t add up. I believed it too. I’m a physical chemist, and for decades I trusted the same dietary guidelines and medical advice as everyone else — while my health came apart. By my mid-sixties I was obese and failing: fatty liver disease, arthritis, chronic fatigue, mental fog, a gallbladder removed in my early fifties, and back pain I’d carried since high school. I was doing everything I’d been told to do. At 66 I changed the way I ate. Within a year I lost 70 pounds. The fatty liver cleared. The back pain went. The fog lifted. The arthritis in my hands disappeared. The pills and painkillers stopped. Five years later, at 71, I take no medications and have had no procedures. When a single change reverses that many conditions the medical system had treated as separate, a chemist has to ask whether they were ever separate at all. That question began over dinner. An old friend told me his own recovery had started with a conversation we’d had more than twenty years earlier — one I couldn’t remember having. A seed I’d planted without knowing it had changed his life, and now he was handing it back to me. That dinner sent me back to first principles. I stopped asking what the guidelines said.
